rv.q: This Fantasticks strikes those ruminative chords quite well, particularly in its achingly gorgeous final tableau.

The charming new Broadway incarnation of The Fantasticks , lovingly directed and choreographed by Christopher Gattelli, has roots in the show's storied past; Jason Sherwood's set begins with a ghost-lit evocation of the original Off Broadway run.
And thus Second Stage’s Hayes Theatre becomes like a little oasis for those with a fondness for green grass, yellow grain and a life more tender and mellow.
This likable staging is not out to make any hard-hitting social statements.
After the pleasures of this Fantasticks , new in some ways yet still, in fact, entirely its old self, what else might we, like Lewis unchastened, dare to imagine?
They, and everything else in this production, work together to bring a theatrical warhorse galloping into 21st Century Broadway, surprising us with just how much pluck it can still carry.

The show basks in quaintness and the magic of traditional theater-making, with its supporting players, expertly portrayed by David Patrick Kelly and Kevin Del Aguila, forming a kind of connective tissue to Shakespeare and vaudeville.
Mr. Gattelli has cast the production with such a wealth of talent that even the fable-phobic can take sustained pleasure in the many wonderful things it does indeed bring.
Christopher Gattelli’s sublime and heart-tugging revival feels like an antidote to an industry that’s increasingly allergic to simple, earnest storytelling.

Her courage in continuing to perform, and in taking on this role in particular, is in itself remarkable, and it lends added resonance to a show that remains a testament to the resilience of love, in all its forms.
This production for Second Stage at the Helen Hayes Theater is loving and uncynical, a sweet little gem that doesn't try to be something it's not by virtue of location.
The structure and soul of the show remain untouched—it’s still a sweet little story about two naive young lovers, their madcap hopes and dreams, and the harsh realities that bring them back to earth.

This first Broadway revival of “The Fantasticks” is blessed with great singing voices and Nevin Steinberg’s amplification supports them without homogenizing those voices into the current loud-arena sound design that infects the rest of Broadway.
Queerness gives the long-running musical’s central romance a tender new sense of wonder.
The moment is just what you hope for in a musical — a heartstopper.
The ballads are heaven, the choral work is intricate and ear-tickling, and it was a particular delight to hear the comic numbers winning such huge laughs.
If you haven’t, I’d catch it while it makes this brief, welcome return to our boards.

This enlargement feels far more intrusive than the change to two boys (rather than a boy and a girl), whose mothers (rather than their fathers) secretly scheme to bring them together by pretending to be in a life-long feud.
The drawback here—it’s not meager—is that the boys’ love affair comes across as tepid.
Still, little is gained and much is lost in the transfer to Broadway of this magical show.

This outstanding reboot of “The Fantasticks” opens and closes with the soaring classic ballad, “Try to Remember,” belted out by El Gallo, the mystical narrator who guides us through their rocky journey.
Christopher Gattelli has not only proven me wrong, but has given me an entirely new appreciation for a show I thought I knew inside and out. This production is positively magical.
Timeless and tender, sentimental and sassy, high-spirited and highly recommended.
I was completely charmed by this production, including its gentle rhythms and its occasional awkward turns.
Ultimately, this wonderful production of The Fantasticks succeeds because it understands that updating a classic doesn’t mean abandoning its heart.

Director-choreographer Christopher Gattelli’s joyous staging maintains the charm, wit, and warmth of this unimpeachable show, even if the move to a bigger stage at times reminds audiences why it succeeded on more intimate ones.
This artfully staged revival conjures a nostalgia for plain storytelling, elegant folk melodies with a hint of classicism, and unembellished romanticism — all in a still somewhat intimate setting.
Each of these performers in this dazzling ensemble steals your heart whenever they erupt into song.

"The Fantasticks" is too much of a playful fable to support what Jones has appended to it; when Matt and Lewis literally walk together hand in hand into the sunset at the finale, the overt sentimentality just rings hollow.
Better put, this is a Fantasticks for the ages.
Second Stage's inventive Broadway revival of this cherished classic offers a wonderful escape from everyday troubles and a chance to spend an enchanted afternoon or evening at the theater.
By not attempting to recreate past productions, “The Fantasticks” revels in new moments of comedy and beauty.

cn.t: This gay reimagining of the world's longest-running musical earns mostly warm notices for its tender boy-meets-boy romance, though some critics question whether the intimate classic fully survives its leap to Broadway.

vs.sum: One of Broadway's smallest houses (597 seats) and one of its newest, built in 2015 as Second Stage's permanent home. The intimate scale means excellent sightlines from nearly every seat, though the modern design prioritizes function over grandeur.
